title: Perf incident postmortem: SLO misses & customer escalation - 2026-03-22
content:
Summary:

On 2026-03-22 we observed sustained SLO misses for hosted text-generation endpoints (p95/p99 token-latency spikes) between 09:10-11:45 UTC, which triggered automated alerts and a customer escalation from Acme AI. This doc captures the investigation, root cause, hotfix(es) we deployed, and validation results.

Impact:
- Affected routes: /v1/generate (cuda-backed quantized models, primarily rwd-3B-int8)
- Customer visible: increased streamed-token latency; some client SDKs reported timeouts for long-running completions
- Internal SLOs impacted: p95 token-latency target (<=150ms) breached; observed p95 ~ 460ms, p99 ~ 1.2s at peak
- Time window: 2026-03-22 09:10-11:45 UTC
- Customers escalated: Acme AI (support ticket SRV-4821) + internal Pager duty pages

Detection and triage timeline (concise):
- 09:11 UTC: alerting SLO process fires (p95 > 250ms for 5m).
- 09:13 UTC: SRE (oncall) begins initial triage, confirms error rates OK but latencies high.
- 09:20 UTC: Customer success escalates - Acme reports timeouts for multi-k request flows.
- 09:30-10:00 UTC: Devs gather traces and flamegraphs from hades-prod-*-pods; initial profiling captured.
- 10:15 UTC: Hotfix candidate identified and rolled to canary (see hotfix details).
- 10:40 UTC: Canary looks stable; start rolling to ~20% traffic.
- 11:05 UTC: Roll to 100% completed; metrics back within SLOs by 11:20 UTC.

What we measured (key signals):
- CPU host-side stalls: increased host-to-device memcpy wait time observed in timeline sampling (avg memcpy wait up ~3x).
- Kernel selection fallback: several models frequently fell back from the fast int8 attention kernel path to a generic attention kernel (slower, more SM-bound).
- Batching queue behavior: continuous-batching queue showed periodic starvation; burst of small requests prevented optimal full-batch consolidation causing more kernel launches.
- KV cache eviction pressure: KV cache GC ran more frequently at the same time window, causing extra memory operations and pauses in request processing.

Root cause analysis (hypothesis + evidence):
1) Regression in kernel selector config introduced 2 failures: a) a mis-detected device capability flag (reported as missing TF32 support for some GPUs) and b) permissive fallback enabled more aggressively. Evidence: commit 9f3a1c7 (serving/runtime/kernel-selector) modified fallback thresholds and landed 2026-03-21 04:18 UTC. Canary metrics after that deploy (nightly) had limited coverage for high concurrency shapes.
2) Combined with a workload shift (Acme started a higher concurrency ramp at 09:00 UTC due to a scheduled batch job), the permissive fallback caused an increase in kernel launch counts + lower per-kernel throughput. Evidence: profiler flamegraphs show attention kernel time/launch count increased 4x; SM utilization decreased from ~65% to ~42% for the slow kernel path.
3) Host-side memcpy increase was secondary: more kernel launches and smaller batches increased PCIe transfers and pinned memory churn, which amplified latency tail. Evidence: async memcpy queue metrics and nvprof snapshots show memcpy_wait_time increase correlating with p99 spikes.

Why the regression wasn't caught earlier:
- Unit + nightly benchmarks tested stable single-shot latency and medium throughput, but did not cover high-concurrency small-request patterns observed in production.
- Kernel selector change lacked a targeted load test for small-batch high-concurrency shapes (we have an open test gap).

Actions taken during incident (short):
- Immediate: Rolled back kernel-selector threshold in canary (revert part of 9f3a1c7) and disabled permissive fallback for int8 attention on affected HW.
- Mitigation: Increased batching window (ms) for an interim period to allow better consolidation of small requests for rwd-3B-int8 routes.
- Customer comms: Support sent interim mitigation steps and ETA; engineering provided an explanation + ETA for hotfix validation.

Hotfix details and validation:
- Hotfix (hotfix/disable-int8-permissive-fallback): pinned the kernel-selector to prefer the verified int8 attention kernel and re-enabled strict capability checks; also added a guard to skip permissive fallback when concurrency > 128.
- Canary validation plan:
  - Load pattern: replayed 2 hours of production traces against canary infra (shape: ~60% small requests (<=16 tokens), 40% medium (<=128 tokens), concurrency up to 200).
  - Key metrics checked: p50/p95/p99 token-latency, kernel-launch counts, memcpy_wait_time, SM utilization, error rates.
- Canary results (10:15-10:35 UTC):
  - p95 dropped from 460ms -> 140ms; p99 from 1.2s -> 260ms.
  - Kernel-launch count per request decreased ~2.7x on average.
  - memcpy_wait_time returned to baseline levels (within 10%).
  - No increase in error rates or resource exhaustion observed.
- Rollout: progressive rollout (10% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%) over 45 minutes with monitoring alarms for regression. Full rollout completed by 11:05 UTC; stabilized by 11:20 UTC.

Post-incident remediation (owners and tickets):
- Short-term (week):
  - SRV-4823 (Marco): Add load tests for small-batch high-concurrency shapes to the nightly perf suite.
  - SRV-4824 (Leah): Harden kernel-selector config to require explicit opt-in for permissive fallback + add feature flag gating per-tenant.
  - SRV-4825 (Anika): Throttle KV cache GC under high concurrency; ensure GC ops are bounded and non-blocking.
- Medium-term (30 days):
  - SRV-4826 (Infra): Improve observability: add per-route kernel-path metrics, hostMemcpy histograms, and batch consolidation ratios to the Console (Per-route dashboards).
  - SRV-4827 (SRE): Add automated canary/chaos testing job that runs high-concurrency small-batch traces on PRs that touch kernel-selector or batching logic.

Follow-up notes / things we learned:
- Kernel selector behavior is effectively a production guardrail; any permissive fallback must be validated with representative load shapes.
- Small-request-heavy workloads are sensitive to batching heuristics; small changes in batching windows can flip cost vs latency trade-offs dramatically.
- Observability gap: we lacked per-route kernel-path telemetry which made root-cause attribution slower.

Appendix: profiling artifacts and quick snippets (links in linked_artifacts):
- Flamegraph (hades-prod-canary-2026-03-22.svg) - shows attention kernel time spike in affected pods.
- nvprof summaries: memcpy_wait_time and kernel_launch_count by PID.
- Sample logs: request-id 8a1f3c (Acme) - shows timeline of queued -> memcpy -> kernel_launch -> completion with delays.

Open questions / TODOs (notes-to-self style):
- Confirm whether permissive fallback was enabled for other model families (Llama variants) - quick audit planned (Marco).
- Decide on default batching-window and publish recommended defaults for dedicated vs hosted tiers.
- Consider a feature flag surface in Console for customers to opt into permissive fallback (with explicit warning).

Owner for postmortem write-up and comms: Jordan Patel (eng-serving-runtime).

Status: in_review - please leave comments, especially on the remediation tickets assigned above.

---
Notes from oncall timeline (raw snippets):
- "10:03 UTC: kernel-selector metrics: fallback_count spike -> 820 in 5m window"
- "10:07 UTC: hotfix canary applied, early signal: p95 trending down"
- "11:20 UTC: all routes green; verify for 24h before closing SRV-4821 with customer"

End of document.
